about: The fish genera's own presentation and ID marks, for the circle-1 genera the IMR fish presentation gives no cues for (Pierre, 2026-11-08: each genus needs a short presentation and its ID cues, sourced, rules C2, C3, C6, before the genera open to more players). Our own words, never copied, written from public sources: src, each {t, u}, t starting with the source's short name before its first comma. families: the families done (every circle-1 genus of these without IMR cues is in genera with marks, or in none with its reason). genera, by genus name: plain, [one or two sentences on what the genus looks like and how it lives, its refs]; marks, 1 to 3 [visible feature that tells it from the other genera of its family, its refs], a ref being [src key, where in it (key couplet or species account, page)]. Only features seen on a photo: never a fin-ray, spine or scale count, nor a feature seen only in the hand; a species named is one of the genus's game species (rule C6). Most lines come from the FAO species identification guide for the Western Central Pacific (Carpenter and Niem, eds, vols 3 and 4, 1999, vols 5 and 6, 2001: each family's key to the genera, or its key to the species where it has none, and its species accounts), the rest from FishBase species pages; a genus the guide names otherwise says so (as Xyrichtys, as Pseudaluteres, as Dendrochirus brachypterus, as Apogon cyanosoma, as Trachinocephalus myops). The only genus of its family here gets a presentation only: the family's IMR cues and ID marks tell it. none: a genus left without marks and why (no visible feature in the sources read): never a mark guessed. A genus with IMR cues is never here: the IMR cues stay apart (rule C1). tools/build_fish.py add_families puts plain, marks, msrc and mby on fish.json genera; app.js fishGenera shows them on the genus card, learn.js genMarks on the sheet the genus opens.

plain: Coral breams live on coral reefs or on sand and mud close to them, down to about 60 m, alone or in groups.
Anthias gather in large groups above coral outcrops to feed on plankton; in P. squamipinnis, females turn into males, which keep harems.
Soldierfishes rest in caves and under ledges by day and come out at night to feed on the larger zooplankton.
